goal: Establish a repeatable conditioning strategy that improves softness, slip and manageability while using protein, lipids and bond-supporting products appropriately.
goal_note: This isn't about switching products at random, or reaching for an intensive protein treatment just because hair feels dry.
pillars: Use rinse-out conditioner after every wash and a deep-conditioning step on the scheduled wash day.
Use water-based conditioning products and leave-in care to support slip, softness and manageability between wash days.
Schedule a ceramide- or lipid-focused treatment to support hair-fiber conditioning and lubrication.
Use protein treatments when the hair's damage history and observed response justify them. Use bond-supporting treatments when chemical or thermal damage warrants them.

explainers: Protein: what it does and what it does not do

Hydrolyzed proteins are used in hair-conditioning products. Their effects depend on factors such as molecular size, formulation, deposition and contact time. They may temporarily improve the feel and performance of hair fibers, which is not the same as permanently rebuilding hair.

"Protein deficiency" and "protein overload" aren't diagnoses you can make from how hair feels. Stiffness, roughness or breakage can have several explanations, including buildup, insufficient conditioning, damage, product incompatibility and handling practices.

Hair fibers contain lipids that contribute to their structure and surface characteristics. Lipid-containing conditioning products can support cosmetic conditioning and improve the feel of damaged hair. The evidence for any one product depends on its formulation, not merely the presence of a ceramide or oil on its ingredient list.

Hair's mechanical properties involve multiple types of bonds and interactions. The research is complex, and product technologies differ. Look at the specific technology and follow the product's directions; no single bond treatment rebuilds every damaged bond.
